lesson.title: Off the End of the List: What IndexError Really Means
lesson.summary: IndexError is what Python raises when code asks a sequence, like a list or a string, for a position that does not exist, and recognizing it quickly is the first step toward writing bounds-safe code.
lesson.body:
Every list and string in Python is a sequence, meaning its items sit in order at whole number positions starting from 0. As covered when you learned string indexing, a sequence of length n has valid positions 0 through n minus 1 when counting from the front, and negative positions -1 through -n when counting from the back. Ask for anything outside that range and Python has no item to hand back, so it raises IndexError, one of the built in exception types.

```python
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95]
print(scores[3])
print(scores[4])
```

scores[3] is a valid position, the last item in a four item list, so it prints 95 without any trouble. scores[4] has no matching position, since the list only has items at positions 0, 1, 2, and 3. Python raises:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
IndexError: list index out of range
```

Strings raise the exact same exception for the exact same reason, since a string is also a sequence, just of characters instead of arbitrary values. "cat"[5] raises IndexError: string index out of range, worded slightly differently but coming from the identical underlying cause: the position you asked for does not exist.

IndexError shows up constantly in ordinary code, usually from one of three habits: a loop condition that goes one step too far, an assumption that a list has at least one item when it might actually be empty, or forgetting that the last valid position is len(sequence) minus 1, not len(sequence) itself. A defensive habit worth building now is checking length before indexing, especially near the edges of a collection.

```python
def get_last(sequence):
    if len(sequence) == 0:
        return None
    return sequence[-1]
```

This same kind of edge, what happens when a list is empty, or has exactly one item, is precisely what you will later learn to check for on purpose with deliberate test cases. For now, the important habit is reading the traceback carefully. When you see IndexError, it is a solid sign the bug lives in exactly one place: wherever a number is being used as a position into a list or a string.
